title: Tiling and scratchpad attention experiments — lab notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploration notes comparing FlashAttention (FA), paged/tiled attention, and a small fused-op prototype that we built in the lab branch. Aim is to identify micro-bottlenecks that cause latency regressions at low-batch low-latency SLOs, and verify where memory-tiling/scratchpad strategies help or hurt for long contexts (>=2k tokens).

Executive summary (short):
- FlashAttention (v2.0 build) gives best latency for small-to-medium seq (<=1024) on A100 for batch sizes 1 and 4.
- For long sequences (>=2048) and large KV caches paged/tiled attention has steadier memory use and sometimes lower p99 due to avoiding large contiguous allocations.
- Our fused matmul+softmax+mul prototype reduces kernel launches by ~30% and improved single-request token latency by ~12% for seq=512, but regressed throughput at batch=16 due to register pressure and lower occupancy.
- Biggest offender for p99 in production-like traces: host<->device memcopies for KV cache growth (un-pinned copies) and kernel launch overhead for many tiny kernels.

Environment / reproducibility notes:
- HW: AWS p4d-equivalent, A100-40GB (PCIe-equivalent test rig), CUDA 11.8 (lab), cudnn 8.4, pytorch 2.1 nightly / custom runtime branch.
- FlashAttention: local build from commit fa-v2.0-2024-09 (patched for 32-bit index fallback).
- Paged attention: our in-house paged-kv implementation (branch: paged-kv-tiling) which splits KV into 256MiB pages and maps active pages into a pre-allocated scratchpool using cuMemMap/cuMemAdvise in prototype.
- Fused ops: small experimental kernel fusing matmul(queries, keys^T) -> softmax -> mul(values). Branch: fused-attn-experiments.
- Profiler: nv-nsight (kernel timeline + memory copy view) + cupy based wall-clock microbench harness for per-token timing. Also used nvtx ranges to correlate steps with serving runtime traces.

Key observations and numbers (representative):
(1) Single-request median token latency (ms/token), A100-40GB, PyTorch dispatch overhead included
- seq=512, batch=1: FlashAttention = 2.8 ms/token; paged-tiling = 3.6 ms/token; fused-proto = 2.5 ms/token
- seq=1024, batch=1: FlashAttention = 4.9 ms/token; paged-tiling = 5.2 ms/token; fused-proto = 4.3 ms/token
- seq=2048, batch=1: FlashAttention = 12.1 ms/token; paged-tiling = 9.8 ms/token; fused-proto = 11.5 ms/token
Notes: for seq>=2048 paged-tiling wins because it avoids the large contiguous scratch allocation and spreads memory traffic across smaller kernels that better fit L2/shared cache patterns.

(2) Throughput/latency tradeoffs at batch=8 (tokens/sec generalized):
- FlashAttention: high throughput at short seq, but backs off quicker as seq grows due to single big kernel causing memory-bandwidth spikes.
- Paged-tiling: lower peak throughput for short seq but better throughput stability for long seq.
- Fused-proto: best latency at small batch but suffers at batch>=16 due to lowered active warps (register/spill).

(3) NVTX / nsight traces: common patterns seen in p99 cases:
- Repeated small H2D memcopies during KV growth (un-pinned malloc + cudaMemcpy) correlate with 30-120ms jitter spikes. We still have code paths where KV page growth triggers host-side memcpy instead of async pinned+stream copy.
- FlashAttention has a long-duration single kernel that occupies SMs for extended periods; during that time small control kernels (e.g., KV snapshot, metrics) queue up and add micro-latency.
- Paged-tiling shows many more kernel launches but shorter kernels — overall lower max-SM-time and fewer long-blocking phases.

Microbench debug traces (excerpt):
- seq=2048 batch=1, p99 timeline snapshot:
  1) H2D memcpy (un-pinned) 12ms — triggered by KV grow
  2) FA kernel (global) 85ms
  3) small control kernel 0.8ms queued behind FA -> p99 increases by 0.8ms per token in worst case
- For paged-tiling same trace:
  1) 6x small page-load async copies (pinned) 6x 2ms each overlapping with compute -> total shows better overlap and p99 ~ (85 - overlap)

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: Host memcopy strategy is the single largest cause of p99 spikes when KV cache growth happens. Fix: always use pinned host buffers + cudaMemcpyAsync + dedicated stream + prefetch into device memory pool. (evidence strong from trace correlation).
- H2: Kernel launch count vs long-kernel tradeoff: long single kernels (like FA) increase queuing latency for short control kernels; tiling reduces kernel time but increases launches which helps interleaving.
- H3: Fused kernels: reduce launches and improve latency at small batch but can regress throughput because of register usage -> lower SM occupancy and L2 evictions.

Things we tried and quick results:
- Switch to pinned host buffers for KV page population: reduced memcopy jitter by ~6x in synthetic test. (PR: linked above).
- Pre-splitting KV allocation into 4x smaller slabs (instead of single big contiguous) -> slightly improved long-ctx latency because reduces fragmentation and makes reuse easier.
- Tuned fused kernel to reduce register usage (compile-time tile size changes) -> restored some throughput but still worse than non-fused at batch>=16. Next step: try persistent threads or multi-block reduction to reduce per-thread register pressure.

Open issues / surprising failures:
- On CUDA 12 dev nodes we saw a kernel launch latency increase vs 11.8 for tiny kernels (~30–50us increase). Not sure if driver-level or our nvcc flags. Reproducible on two different machines. Ticketed (INF-4523).
- cuMemMap-based scratchpool prototype works, but fragmentation and NUMA interactions on multi-socket hosts cause page eviction stalls on heavy multi-tenant runs. Need longer soak tests.
- When switching to fused-op on older GPU (v100 equivalently), the kernel fails with register spill causing out-of-memory at compile time — indicates our tile params are too aggressive. Need parameter sweep per-arch.

Actionable next steps (short list):
- (short) Enforce pinned host copy path for all KV growth operations — low-effort high-impact. Owner: Arjun. ETA: 1 week.
- (mid) Add an async KV page prefetcher triggered by request predicted active pages (heuristic: lookahead tokens). Owner: Samir. ETA: 3 weeks for prototype.
- (mid) Run occupancy and register-pressure tuning for fused kernel per-arch; fallback to unfused kernel when occupancy drops below threshold. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2 weeks for parameter sweep + perf dashboard.
- (investigate) Kernel launch overhead regression on CUDA12 nodes — coordinate with infra/engineering to capture driver+nvcc flags and file issue with vendor if needed. Owner: Lena. ETA: 2 weeks.

Experiments to add (ideas):
- Microbenchmark: run synthetic mixes that mimic production token-length distribution and measure memcopy patterns + p99 before/after pinned-copy fix.
- Hybrid runtime: route short-ctx requests to FA path and long-ctx to paged-tiling automatically based on seq threshold; measure overall p99 and cost. If stable, add routing policy in runtime.
- Evaluate persistent-thread kernels (like persistent-softmax) as alternative to single huge kernel to reduce kernel launch backpressure for control kernels.

Notes to self / rough TODOs in doc form: 
- Capture full nv-nsight traces for 10 p99 spikes, store in /perf/traces/tiling-2024-10 
- Add unit to microbench harness that simulates KV-growth at random token times (to reproduce jitter easily)
- Clean up fused prototype and isolate builder flags that changed register allocation unexpectedly

References and pointers:
- FlashAttention upstream commit used: fa-v2.0-2024-09 (local patch list attached in PR)
- Internal PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987 — includes pinned-copy change and microbench harness commit
- JIRA: INF-4523 — kernel-launch-latency-cuda12 notes

Closing thought: for production SLOs we probably should not force a single universal attention kernel. A hybrid routing strategy (FA for short/medium, paged-tiling for long) + mandatory pinned async copy path for KV population gives the best practical balance between latency and stability. Fused kernels are promising in the small-request case but require careful occupancy fallbacks.

Unresolved questions to discuss in next sync:
- Do we accept extra kernel-launch count (paged approach) as a long-term tradeoff for lower p99?
- Is it acceptable to add a routing policy complexity in runtime (thresholds per-model/arch) or should runtime push for a single canonical kernel?
- How aggressively do we auto-fallback fused vs unfused based on occupancy heuristics?
